lessons.title: Pre-Slaughter Handling and Welfare
lessons.body: Pre-slaughter handling starts 24 hours before killing. Stop feeding your grasscutters 12 to 18 hours before slaughter, but keep clean water available at all times. This empties the stomach, reduces contamination risk during evisceration, and makes the meat safer. Do not starve them longer than 24 hoursâit causes stress and tough meat. Handle animals calmly. Grasscutters are easily frightened; shouting, chasing, or rough grabbing raises stress hormones that make meat dark, dry, and fast to spoil. Move them slowly using a catching net or a calm hand behind the neck. Never lift by the tail or ears. Transport to the slaughter area in a crate with ventilation, one animal per small compartment if possible. Keep the area quiet and shaded. In hot African climates, slaughter in the early morning or late evening when temperatures are below 25Â°C. Heat stress before death ruins meat quality. Provide a clean, non-slip floor. A stressed grasscutter may bite or scratch, so wear thick gloves and long sleeves. Check for signs of illness: runny nose, diarrhoea, or dull eyes. Do not slaughter sick animals for human consumptionâsell or cull them separately. If you must transport, do it gently and avoid long journeys. A 30-minute trip is fine; anything over 2 hours needs rest and water before slaughter. Always have a stunning tool readyâa sharp blow to the head or a captive boltâto render the animal unconscious instantly. This is not cruelty; it is good welfare and produces better meat. Remember, calm animals bleed out faster and yield cleaner carcasses. Train your workers to be patient. One rough handler can ruin a whole batch. Keep records: date, time, animal ID, and any stress signs. This helps you improve. Finally, never slaughter in front of other grasscutters. They panic and release stress hormones. Use a separate room or a screen. Good pre-slaughter care takes only a few extra minutes but pays off in meat quality, shelf life, and customer trust.

lessons.title: Humane Slaughter Methods
lessons.body: Humane slaughter means making the animal unconscious instantly, then bleeding it out quickly. For grasscutters, the two approved methods are blunt force trauma to the head and captive bolt stunning. Blunt force: use a heavy wooden club or a metal pipe wrapped in rubber. Strike a single, hard blow to the back of the head, just behind the ears, at the base of the skull. The animal should collapse immediately, with no eye blink or righting reflex. If it blinks or tries to stand, you missedâstrike again immediately. Captive bolt: a tool that fires a retractable bolt into the skull. It is expensive but reliable. Place the bolt flat against the forehead, slightly above eye level, and fire. The animal drops instantly. After stunning, immediately hang the animal by its hind legs on a gambrel or a strong hook. Use a sharp, clean knifeâa 15 cm boning knife or a slaughter knife. Cut the throat deeply behind the jawbone, severing the carotid arteries and jugular veins. Let the blood drain for 3 to 5 minutes into a bucket. Do not cut the windpipe if you want to keep the head for by-products. Bleeding must be thorough; residual blood makes meat spoil faster and gives a gamey taste. Never slaughter without stunningâit causes pain and stress hormones. Do not use drowning or suffocation; these are cruel and illegal in many countries. For small-scale farmers, blunt force is cheap and effective if done correctly. Practice on a dead animal or a dummy first. Keep your tools sharp and clean. After bleeding, the carcass is ready for skinning. Work on a clean table or a hanging rail. Wear gloves and an apron. Wash your hands and knives with soap and water between animals. If you slaughter multiple grasscutters, do one at a time. Always have a backup stunning tool in case the first fails. Record the time of stunning and bleeding. A good slaughter takes less than 2 minutes from stun to bleed-out. Remember, a humane death is not just ethicalâit produces better meat that customers prefer. Train your workers and supervise until they are skilled.

lessons.title: Skinning and Evisceration
lessons.body: Skinning and evisceration must be done quickly and cleanly. Start within 5 minutes after bleeding. Hang the carcass by the hind legs at about waist height. Use a sharp knife to cut a ring around each hind leg at the hock joint. Then cut a straight line from the hock down the inner thigh to the tail, and another line from the tail up the belly to the chest. Do not cut into the meatâkeep the blade angled slightly outward. Peel the skin down like a jacket. Grasscutter skin is thick and tough, so use pliers or a skinning hook to pull it off. Work from the hind legs toward the head. Cut the skin around the front legs and neck. The skin should come off in one piece. Save it for by-products. Once skinned, open the belly carefully. Make a small cut just below the breastbone, then insert two fingers to guide the knife and avoid puncturing the intestines. Cut all the way to the tail. Remove the intestines, stomach, liver, heart, and lungs. Pull them out gently into a bucket. Do not rupture the intestinesâif you do, wash the carcass immediately with clean water and vinegar. Separate the edible organs: liver, heart, and kidneys are good for sale or home use. The stomach and intestines can be cleaned and used as casings for sausages. Remove the head at the base of the skull if you want to sell it separately. Cut off the feet at the ankle joint. Rinse the carcass inside and out with clean, cool water. Use a brush to scrub any blood or dirt. Then hang the carcass to dry for 10 minutes. Do not soak in waterâit makes meat soggy. Work on a stainless steel or plastic table. Never use woodâit harbours bacteria. Clean and sanitise all tools and surfaces after each carcass. Wear gloves and wash hands often. If you are not selling immediately, chill the carcass to 4Â°C within 2 hours. Skinning and evisceration should take 15 to 20 minutes per animal once you are skilled. Practice makes perfect.

lessons.title: Carcass Evaluation and Grading
lessons.body: Carcass evaluation helps you set a fair price and know your product quality. After evisceration, weigh the warm carcass. A good grasscutter carcass should be 1.5 to 2.5 kg for a mature animal. Dressing percentage is carcass weight divided by live weight, times 100. Aim for 55% to 60%. If it is below 50%, the animal was too fat or too thin. Look at the meat colour: fresh grasscutter meat is light pink to pale red, with white fat. Dark, brownish meat means the animal was stressed or old. Check the fat cover: a thin layer of fat over the back and kidneys is ideal. Too much fat means waste; too little means dry meat. Feel the firmness: press the thigh muscleâit should spring back. Soft, watery meat is a sign of poor handling or disease. Inspect for bruises, abscesses, or parasites. Any green or yellow spots on the liver mean diseaseâdiscard the liver. Grade your carcasses into three classes: Grade A (1.8â2.5 kg, well-fleshed, light pink, no blemishes), Grade B (1.2â1.8 kg, moderate flesh, slight blemishes), Grade C (under 1.2 kg, thin, dark meat, or defects). Grade A fetches the highest price, up to 30% more than Grade C. Sell Grade A to hotels and restaurants. Grade B to local markets. Grade C for home consumption or processing into sausages and stews. Keep a record sheet: date, animal ID, live weight, carcass weight, dressing %, grade, and any remarks. This helps you track breeding and feeding performance. If you see many Grade C carcasses, improve your feed or health programme. Always evaluate in good light. Use a clean, white surface. Weigh with a hanging scale or a digital bench scale. Do not guessâaccurate weights build customer trust. Finally, show your grading system to buyers. They will pay more for consistent quality.

lessons.title: Meat Handling and Storage
lessons.body: After grading, meat must be handled hygienically to prevent spoilage. In hot African climates, bacteria multiply fast. Cool the carcass quickly. If you have a refrigerator, set it to 0â4Â°C and hang the carcass for 12â24 hours. This ages the meat, making it tender. If you have no fridge, use a cool box with ice packs. Or dig a pit, line it with clean plastic, and place the meat inside, covered with wet cloths. Change the cloths every 2 hours. Never leave meat in the sun. Cut the carcass into pieces: legs, shoulders, ribs, and loin. Use a clean knife and a plastic cutting board. Wash your hands and knives with soap and hot water between cuts. Wear gloves. Pack meat in clean plastic bags or containers. Label with date and weight. For short-term storage (up to 3 days), keep at 4Â°C. For longer storage, freeze at -18Â°C. Frozen meat keeps 6â12 months. Never refreeze thawed meatâit spoils quickly. If you sell fresh meat, keep it on ice at the market. Use a clean white cloth to cover it. Do not let flies land on meat. Use a screen or a fan. For transport, use a cool box with ice. Keep the box closed. Sell within 4 hours. If you smoke or dry meat, follow safe methods. Smoking: use a closed smoker at 60â70Â°C for 4â6 hours. Drying: cut meat into thin strips, salt lightly, and dry in a solar dryer or in the sun under a net. Dried meat keeps for months. Always wash your hands before handling meat. Clean all surfaces with bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water). Never mix raw meat with cooked food. Store raw meat at the bottom of the fridge. If you see slime, smell ammonia, or see green spots, throw the meat away. Do not sell spoiled meatâit can kill. Train your workers on hygiene. A clean operation sells more meat.

lessons.title: Value Addition and By-Products
lessons.body: Value addition turns a 2 kg carcass into more income. Instead of selling whole, process into sausages, smoked meat, or ready-to-cook cuts. Sausages: use 70% grasscutter meat, 20% pork fat, and 10% spices (salt, pepper, garlic, nutmeg). Grind, stuff into cleaned grasscutter intestines or synthetic casings, and smoke at 70Â°C for 2 hours. Sell at 2â3 times the price of fresh meat. Smoked meat: rub pieces with salt, pepper, and paprika. Smoke over hardwood (not pine) for 4â6 hours. Vacuum-pack for longer shelf life. Dried meat (biltong): cut thin strips, marinate in vinegar, salt, and spices for 12 hours, then air-dry for 2â3 days. Sell as a snack. By-products: the skin can be tanned into leather for bags, belts, or drum covers. Tan with alum and saltâsearch online for simple recipes. The head and feet can be cooked into soup or stew. The liver, heart, and kidneys are delicaciesâsell separately. The blood can be cooked into a thick porridge (like African blood sausage). The bones can be boiled for stock or ground into bone meal for poultry feed. The fat can be rendered into cooking oil or soap. Even the tail can be sold as a lucky charm in some markets. To add value, invest in a small grinder (hand-crank or electric), a sausage stuffer, and a vacuum sealer. Package attractively with a label: your farm name, weight, and date. Sell to restaurants, supermarkets, and online. Train your staff on food safety. Keep records of costs and profits. A single grasscutter can yield 1.5 kg of meat, 0.5 kg of by-products, and 1 skin. If you sell all, you can double your income. Start smallâtry one product at a time. Test the market. Ask customers what they want. Then scale up. Value addition is the key to a profitable grasscutter business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Slaughtering and Processing Grasscutters for Profit

Slaughtering and processing is where grasscutter farming stops being a livestock project and becomes a food business. Every decision at this stage â how you handle animals before slaughter, how cleanly you work, how well you chill and package â determines your yield, your shelf life, your price per kilogram, and whether buyers come back. In West and Central Africa, where grasscutter (Thryonomys swinderianus) meat commands a premium in urban markets, hotels and restaurants, the difference between a profitable processor and a marginal one is usually hygiene, consistency and value addition, not scale.

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into field-ready guidance. Use it as a bench manual: keep it near your slaughter area, train staff against it, and audit yourself weekly.

Pre-Slaughter Handling and Welfare

Withdraw feed 12â24 hours before slaughter but keep clean water available. This reduces gut content, lowers contamination risk during evisceration, and improves carcass hygiene. Never transport or slaughter visibly stressed animals â stress depletes muscle glycogen, raising final pH and producing dark, firm, dry (DFD) meat that spoils faster and fetches lower prices. Handle animals quietly, one at a time, in shaded holding pens. In hot African climates, hold animals off concrete during the hottest hours to prevent heat stress. A calm animal bleeds out faster and more completely, which directly improves meat quality and shelf life.

Humane Slaughter Methods

Humane slaughter is both an ethical and a commercial requirement. Use a quick, decisive method: mechanical stunning followed by immediate bleeding, or cervical dislocation for small stock where permitted by local regulations. For grasscutters, a sharp blow to the base of the skull followed by severing the jugular vein and carotid artery is widely used. Bleed over a collection tray â blood is a saleable by-product (see Value Addition). Ensure one trained person performs slaughter consistently; inconsistent technique causes bruising, bone damage and blood spots that downgrade carcasses.

Skinning and Evisceration

Work on a clean, washable surface. Hang the carcass by the hind legs, make a circular cut around the hocks and a midline incision, then pull the skin downward. Grasscutter skin is thick and can be tanned (see by-products). After skinning, open the abdomen carefully â do not puncture the intestines or stomach. Remove all viscera, keeping the liver, heart and kidneys if the animal was healthy. Wash the carcass with clean, potable water, not stagnant water. Inspect for abscesses, parasites or lesions; condemn any carcass showing signs of disease. Weigh the carcass and record it â this is your yield data.

Carcass Evaluation and Grading

Grading drives price. Buyers pay more for uniform, well-fleshed, blemish-free carcasses. Evaluate on conformation, fat cover, meat colour and dressing percentage. Dressing percentage for grasscutter typically falls in the 50â60% range depending on age, sex and condition. Record every carcass so you can benchmark your herd's performance.

Table 1. Indicative grasscutter carcass grading criteria
GradeConformationFat CoverMeat ColourTypical Use
A (Premium)Well-muscled, uniformModerate, evenBright redHotels, premium retail
B (Standard)Moderate musclingSlightRedRestaurants, markets
C (Processing)Thin, unevenMinimalDark redSmoking, sausages, stews

Source: Adapted from FAO (1994) Manual on Simple Methods of Meat Preservation, and FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius meat hygiene guidance â fao.org/3/x6932e.

Meat Handling and Storage

Time and temperature are your two enemies. Chill carcasses to 0â4Â°C within two hours of slaughter. In off-grid settings, use a chest freezer with a backup or a charcoal/evaporative cooler for short holding. Never stack warm carcasses. Keep raw meat separate from cooked or ready-to-eat products. Use food-grade gloves, sanitised knives and clean aprons. For frozen storage at â18Â°C, grasscutter meat keeps 6â9 months if properly wrapped; chilled meat should move within 3â5 days.

Table 2. Recommended storage times and temperatures for grasscutter meat
Storage MethodTemperatureMax Shelf LifeNotes
Chilled (fresh)0â4Â°C3â5 daysWrap to prevent drying
Frozenâ18Â°C or below6â9 monthsVacuum or tight wrap
Hot-smokedAmbient (cool, dry)2â4 weeksProperly dried, sealed
Salted/driedAmbient (cool, dry)1â3 monthsTraditional preservation

Source: FAO (1994) Manual on Simple Methods of Meat Preservation and FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius Code of Hygienic Practice for Meat (CAC/RCP 58-2005) â fao.org/fao-who-codexalimentarius.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Zoonotic and Hygiene Risk

Grasscutters can carry zoonotic pathogens and parasites. Always wear gloves and eye protection during slaughter and evisceration. Never eat, drink or smoke in the slaughter area. Disinfect knives, tables and hands between carcasses. Condemn and safely dispose of any carcass with abscesses, unusual lesions or off odours â do not sell downgraded or suspect meat. Wash hands with soap after handling animals or raw meat. If you develop fever, wounds or illness after handling, seek medical attention promptly.

Value Addition and By-Products

This is where margin lives. Instead of selling whole carcasses, portion into cuts (hind legs, forelegs, loin, ribs), vacuum-pack and label with weight, date and farm name. Process into smoked meat, peppered dried meat, sausages or ready-to-cook marinated packs for urban customers. By-products: skin can be tanned into leather for belts, bags and drum heads; blood can be cooked into blood meal or traditional dishes; bones into bone meal for poultry feed; offal sold fresh or processed. A farm that sells only whole carcasses leaves 30â50% of potential revenue on the table.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Withdraw feed 12â24 hours pre-slaughter; provide clean water.
  2. Handle animals calmly; slaughter in shade, one at a time.
  3. Stun humanely, bleed immediately and completely.
  4. Use clean, sanitised knives, tables and gloves throughout.
  5. Chill carcasses to 0â4Â°C within two hours.
  6. Weigh, grade and record every carcass for yield tracking.
  7. Separate raw and cooked products; maintain cold chain.
  8. Portion, package and add value before selling.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Manual on Simple Methods of Meat Preservation
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Codes of Practice (Meat Hygiene)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (slaughter & welfare)
  • FAO â Good Practices for the Meat Industry
  • IFAD â Rural Value Chain and Market Access Resources

Business note: Treat this module as your quality system. Farms that standardise slaughter, chilling and packaging consistently earn 20â40% more per kilogram than those selling informally. Train staff, document yields, and reinvest in cold chain and packaging â that is how grasscutter farming becomes a real agribusiness.

quiz.q: How long before slaughter should you stop feeding a grasscutter?
quiz.explanation: Stopping feed 12â18 hours before slaughter empties the stomach and reduces contamination risk without causing excessive stress.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended transport time for a grasscutter before slaughter without rest?
quiz.explanation: Trips longer than 2 hours require rest and water to prevent stress and poor meat quality.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a sick grasscutter that should not be slaughtered for human consumption?
quiz.explanation: Runny nose and diarrhoea indicate illness, and such animals should not be slaughtered for human consumption.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid slaughtering a grasscutter in front of others?
options: B) It causes stress hormones in the others
C) It makes the meat taste better
quiz.explanation: Witnessing slaughter causes panic and stress hormone release in other grasscutters, reducing meat quality.

quiz.q: What is the correct target area for blunt force stunning of a grasscutter?
options: B) Base of the skull behind the ears
quiz.explanation: A single hard blow to the base of the skull behind the ears renders the animal instantly unconscious.

quiz.q: After stunning, how long should you wait before bleeding the animal?
quiz.explanation: Bleeding should be done immediately after stunning to ensure quick death and good meat quality.

quiz.q: Which blood vessels should be severed during bleeding?
options: B) Carotid arteries and jugular veins
quiz.explanation: Cutting the carotid arteries and jugular veins ensures rapid and complete bleed-out.

quiz.q: Why is it important to bleed the animal thoroughly?
options: A) It makes the meat lighter
B) It reduces spoilage and gamey taste
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Residual blood promotes spoilage and gives a strong gamey taste; thorough bleeding improves shelf life and flavour.

quiz.q: What is the recommended time from stunning to bleed-out completion?
quiz.explanation: A good slaughter takes less than 2 minutes from stun to bleed-out for optimal welfare and meat quality.

quiz.q: Which tool is recommended for stunning if you can afford it?
quiz.explanation: A captive bolt is a reliable and humane stunning tool, though blunt force is a cheaper alternative.

quiz.q: When should skinning begin after bleeding?
quiz.explanation: Skinning should start within 5 minutes after bleeding to prevent the skin from tightening and to reduce bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What is the first cut made during skinning?
options: A) A ring around each hind leg at the hock
B) A cut along the belly
C) A cut around the neck
D) A cut at the tail
quiz.explanation: Cutting a ring around each hind leg at the hock joint allows you to start peeling the skin downward.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid cutting into the meat while skinning?
options: B) It reduces the carcass value and introduces bacteria
quiz.explanation: Cutting into meat damages the carcass, lowers its grade, and can introduce bacteria from the skin.

quiz.q: What should you do if you accidentally puncture the intestines during evisceration?
options: B) Wash the carcass with clean water and vinegar
quiz.explanation: Washing immediately with clean water and vinegar helps reduce bacterial contamination from spilled gut contents.

quiz.q: Which organs are considered edible and can be sold separately?
quiz.explanation: Liver, heart, and kidneys are delicacies and can be sold for additional income.

quiz.q: What is the ideal dressing percentage for a grasscutter carcass?
quiz.explanation: A dressing percentage of 55â60% indicates good fleshing and proper finishing.

quiz.q: What does dark, brownish meat indicate?
options: B) The animal was stressed or old
quiz.explanation: Dark meat is a sign of stress before slaughter or advanced age, both of which reduce quality.

quiz.q: Which grade of carcass should be sold to hotels and restaurants?
quiz.explanation: Grade A carcasses are well-fleshed, light pink, and free of blemishes, making them ideal for high-end buyers.

quiz.q: What is the weight range for a Grade A grasscutter carcass?
quiz.explanation: Grade A carcasses typically weigh between 1.8 and 2.5 kg, indicating good growth and finish.

quiz.q: How much more can a Grade A carcass fetch compared to Grade C?
quiz.explanation: Grade A carcasses can sell for up to 30% more than Grade C due to superior quality.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time fresh meat can be kept at 4Â°C?
quiz.explanation: At 4Â°C, fresh meat can be stored safely for up to 3 days before spoilage risk increases.

quiz.q: What is the recommended freezer temperature for long-term meat storage?
quiz.explanation: -18Â°C is the standard temperature for freezing meat to preserve it for 6â12 months.

quiz.q: Why should you never refreeze thawed meat?
options: B) It spoils quickly due to bacterial growth
quiz.explanation: Thawing allows bacteria to multiply; refreezing does not kill them, leading to rapid spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a safe method to keep meat cool without a refrigerator?
options: B) Use a cool box with ice packs
quiz.explanation: A cool box with ice packs maintains a low temperature to slow bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What bleach concentration is recommended for sanitising meat surfaces?
quiz.explanation: A solution of 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres of water is effective for sanitising food contact surfaces.

quiz.q: What is a key ingredient in grasscutter sausages besides meat?
quiz.explanation: Pork fat is added to grasscutter sausages to improve texture and moisture.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you smoke meat for value addition?
quiz.explanation: Smoking at 60â70Â°C for several hours safely preserves and flavours the meat.

quiz.q: Which by-product can be tanned into leather?
quiz.explanation: The skin can be tanned using alum and salt to produce leather for bags, belts, and other items.

quiz.q: What can be made from grasscutter blood?
quiz.explanation: Blood can be cooked into a thick porridge or used in blood sausage, a traditional delicacy.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to add value to grasscutter meat?
quiz.explanation: Processing meat into sausages, smoked meat, or dried meat increases income per animal.
